The MD5 and exact size PRIDE recorded for each file deposited in a project

pride_file_checksums.Rd

List the MD5 and exact size PRIDE recorded for each file deposited in a project: the record a downloaded file is checked against.

Answers is the file on my disk the file PRIDE holds? A file is PRIDE's when its length is size_bytes and its MD5 is md5. pride_download and pride_download_files check neither yet, so for files that matter, check them yourself: file.size() and tools::md5sum() are all it takes, as the example shows.

Usage

pride_file_checksums(accession, timeout = NULL)

Arguments

accession

A project accession, e.g. "PXD000001". Upper-cased and trimmed first, because PRIDE's checksum route is case-sensitive.

timeout

Seconds to allow for the whole call. NULL, the default, adds no limit of mzLibR's own, because mzLib already bounds every request: it retries a transient failure three times, after 5, 20 and 60 s, and each attempt can take up to 100 s. An outage that hangs is therefore reported as mzlib_service_unavailable after about 8 minutes per request, and an empty list costs a second request, the project lookup. A number cuts the whole call off after that many seconds with mzlib_timeout, which is not mzlib_service_unavailable.

Details

This is a third list, not a view of either of the others. It covers the files the submitter deposited at the project's root. PRIDE's own generated/ files have no row: a file without a row cannot be checked, and that does not make it invalid. It names files pride_list_files omits (5 of PXD000001's 12 rows on 2026-10-21). And it can name files that are not deposits at all: PXD015239's lists an NFS temp file, .nfs80360b91005fae5300002478. Look up the files you have by name; do not read the list as the project's contents.

The checksum column of pride_list_files is not this MD5. Where PRIDE fills it in, it is a 40-character SHA-1, and for every PXD000001 file it is empty.

Value

A data.frame with one row per file, in file-name order, and the columns file_name, md5, size_bytes and project_accession. Its row names are the file names, so checksums["README.txt", ] looks a file up by the name it was downloaded under; they are case-sensitive, as PRIDE's names are.

file_name is the bare file name, spelled as pride_list_files spells it, never a path. md5 is 32 hexadecimal characters as PRIDE wrote them: lower case in every list seen, but not rewritten, so compare without regard to case (tools::md5sum() is lower case). size_bytes is the file's exact size in bytes, the length a download of it comes to, as a double (raw files pass 2 GiB). Compare a downloaded file's file.size() with it, not with file_size_bytes from pride_list_files, which can differ: for PXD000001's PRIDE_Exp_Complete_Ac_22134.xml.gz that one is 10,677,205 bytes and this one is 10,668,000, the length the download has. project_accession is the accession the list was fetched for.

Zero rows when the project exists but PRIDE holds no checksums for it: that is an answer, not an error, though nothing can then be checked. An unknown accession raises mzlib_project_not_found, and so does a project not yet published, since PRIDE holds no checksums before publication. A list mzLib cannot read (a new header, a malformed row, a name listed twice) stays an mzlib_bridge_error with error_type "MzLibException": the project exists and its list is broken, so "check for a typo" would send you looking for the wrong mistake.

Checking a download

Check both the length and the MD5. The length costs nothing; the MD5 reads the whole file. The length alone does not prove the bytes: on 7 and 8 October 2026, EBI served about 23 of about 70 large transfers at the right size with its own error text written over part of them (mzLib #1449). The PRIDE article shows the check on two damaged copies of a file.

Wraps

Wire verb pride checksums. Generated from the bridge's verb spec pride.checksums.yaml (bridge commit 84c3b984b6b9) by scripts/build-man.R; the spec owns these facts, and all three bindings render the same ones.

  • PrideArchiveClient.GetFileChecksumsAsync in mzLib/UsefulProteomicsDatabases/PrideArchiveClient.cs at mzLib d10017ce

  • PrideFileChecksum in mzLib/UsefulProteomicsDatabases/PrideFileChecksum.cs at mzLib d10017ce

  • PrideArchiveClient.GetProjectAsync in mzLib/UsefulProteomicsDatabases/PrideArchiveClient.cs at mzLib d10017ce

Parameters: units, ranges and defaults

accession

string; required. The project accession, e.g. PXD000001. Sent to PRIDE as given: the bridge checks only that it is not blank. PRIDE's checksum and project routes are case-sensitive (pxd000001 is an unknown accession there), so the bindings upper-case it and check its shape first.

Returned fields

Each field with its type, its unit, and what NA means when it is NA.

project_accession (wire accession)

string; never NA. The accession, echoed as given.

file_count

int; in files; never NA. Entries in files. 0 means the project exists and PRIDE holds no checksum for any of its files, so nothing can be checked. It is an answer, not a not-found: PRIDE answers an unknown accession with an empty list too, so mzLib then asks for the project and fails when there is none (see errors).

files

object[]; never NA. One entry per file, sorted by file_name in ordinal order. mzLib returns a map keyed by file name, which has no order, so the bridge sorts it to send the same list the same way on every run. Fields under result.columns.

Columns

file_name

string; never NA. The bare file name, as pride files spells file_name. Never a path. Unique in the list and case-sensitive: README.txt and readme.txt would be two files.

md5

string; never NA. The file's MD5 as 32 hexadecimal characters, as PRIDE wrote it. Lower case in every list seen, but not rewritten, so compare it without regard to case, as mzLib's own checks do. Not pride files' checksum, which is a different digest (see caveats).

size_bytes

int; in bytes; never NA. The file's exact size in bytes: the length a download of it comes to. A 64-bit count; raw files pass 2 GiB. Compare a downloaded file's length with this, not with pride files' file_size_bytes or pride ftp-files' approximate_size_bytes (see caveats).

Errors

Each is an R condition carrying the class shown and mzlib_error; see mzlib_error.

mzlib_usage_error (usage)

accession missing, blank, or given without a value (checked by the bridge before mzLib)

mzlib_service_unavailable (service_unavailable)

the bridge's own classification (Program.ClassifyError; since mzLib 1.0.593 (#1350) PRIDE raises every transport failure as an HttpRequestException carrying the cause or the status): a timeout or cancellation, a socket failure, an HttpRequestException with no status but an inner cause (refused connection, DNS, TLS), an HTTP 408, 429 or 5xx on the checksum list or on the project lookup, or a body cut off in transit

mzlib_bridge_error (correctness)

no project has that accession, or it is not yet public (MzLibException 'PRIDE Archive has no project with accession ...': PRIDE answers both with an empty list and 404 on the project; the bindings re-map this one message to their not-found error); a list mzLib cannot read (MzLibException, never retried: a header other than File-Name, File-MD5Checksum and File-Size, an empty line before the last row, a row without exactly three tab-separated fields or without a name, an MD5 that is not 32 hexadecimal characters, a size that is not a whole number of bytes, or a name listed twice); any other HTTP status on either request (e.g. 404 on the list)

Caveats

  • Since mzLib 1.0.594 (#1412), PrideArchiveClient retries a transient failure, that request alone, after 5, 20 and 60 s (a 429 or 503 Retry-After of up to 60 s replaces the wait); transient means no HTTP status at all, 408, 429, any 5xx, or a 403 from ftp.pride.ebi.ac.uk, EBI's rate limit. Each attempt can take up to the client's 100 s timeout, so a service that hangs takes up to about 485 s per request before the failure is reported. An empty list costs a second request, the project lookup, with its own retries. A binding's own timeout shorter than that reports a hanging outage as a timeout, not as service_unavailable.

  • A third list, not a view of pride files or pride ftp-files. It covers the files the submitter deposited at the project's root. PRIDE's generated/ files have no row, so a file without a row cannot be checked; that does not make it invalid. For PXD000001 on 2026-10-21 it had 12 rows for the 14 files of the FTP tree (the two missing are in generated/), and 5 of the 12 named files the REST manifest omits.

  • It can list files that are not deposits: PXD015239's includes an NFS temp file, .nfs80360b91005fae5300002478, at 2285905384 bytes. Look up the files you have by name; do not read the list as the project's contents.

  • PRIDE holds no checksums before publication: a project not yet public is the not-found error here, not an empty list.

  • md5 is not pride files' checksum. That field, where PRIDE fills it in, is a 40-character SHA-1 (PXD010820's Maxquant_Output.zip, checked against the downloaded file on 2026-10-21), and for every PXD000001 file it is empty. Do not compare the two.

  • size_bytes is the exact download length, which neither other listing gives. pride files' file_size_bytes can differ: for PXD000001's PRIDE_Exp_Complete_Ac_22134.xml.gz it is 10677205 where the download is 10668000 bytes (this list's value, and an HTTP HEAD's Content-Length on 2026-10-21), and for a .gz file it can be more than ten times larger (PXD015239's 190712-VL-BR-LFQ-1.mzid.gz, per mzLib's PrideFileChecksum). pride ftp-files' sizes are rounded.

  • pride download does not use this list. It calls DownloadProjectFilesAsync, which takes the DownloadFileAsync overload without a checksum, so no size, MD5 or EBI error-page check reaches it (pride thread, PRIDE-B5). Compare a downloaded file's size and MD5 with its row yourself.

  • No total size is sent. mzLib has none over this list, and a sum made in the bridge would be the bridge's number, not mzLib's; sum size_bytes yourself.

Performance

Every call starts one bridge process, which costs a .NET start-up before any work.

Same verb in other bindings

  • Python (pyMzLib): pymzlib.pride.file_checksums

  • Rust (mzLibRust): mzlib::pride::file_checksums_with

  • R (mzLibR): pride_file_checksums

Since

Wire protocol 1; pyMzLib 0.6.0; mzLibRust 0.1.0; mzLibR 0.1.0.

Not yet verified

The spec records these as open. They are listed rather than hidden:

  • mzLib checks that the project exists only when the list's body is empty. A body that is only the header returns 0 rows without that check, so a header-only answer for an unknown accession would read as a project with no checksums. PRIDE has not been seen to send one: it answers an unknown accession with an empty body (PXD999999999, 2026-10-21).

  • No public project with an empty list has been found, so the 0-row answer is pinned by a stubbed test only, not by a recorded fixture.

References

  • doi:10.1093/nar/gkae1011: The PRIDE Archive, whose checksum list this verb reads (Perez-Riverol et al., The PRIDE database at 20 years: 2025 update, NAR)

See also

pride_list_files, pride_download_files

Examples


checksums <- pride_file_checksums("PXD000001")
nrow(checksums)
#> [1] 12
checksums["README.txt", c("md5", "size_bytes")]
#>                                         md5 size_bytes
#> README.txt 492753137013825025e6729c8798664f       1645

# A downloaded file is PRIDE's when both match. Here, a copy cut short:
copy <- tempfile(fileext = ".txt")
writeBin(charToRaw(strrep("x", 1000)), copy)
file.size(copy) == checksums["README.txt", "size_bytes"]
#> [1] FALSE
tolower(unname(tools::md5sum(copy))) == tolower(checksums["README.txt", "md5"])
#> [1] FALSE
unlink(copy)
